# Editorial overview

| Problem | Pattern | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| A. Expected Prize | linearity | `sum v_i p_i/q_i` |
| B. First Success | geometric wait | `q/p` |
| C. Coupon Collector | staged waits | `n * H_n` |

# A. Expected Prize

## Restatement

Each event gives `v[i]` points with probability `p[i]/q[i]`. Compute expected
total points modulo `MOD`.

## Algorithm

For each event:

```text
contribution = v[i] * p[i] * inverse(q[i])
```

Sum all contributions.

## Correctness proof

Let `Xi` be the points from event `i`. It equals `v[i]` with probability
`p[i]/q[i]` and `0` otherwise, so `E[Xi] = v[i]p[i]/q[i]`. By linearity of
expectation, the expected total is the sum of these values. Modular inverses
represent the rational divisions exactly under prime modulus. `\square`

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;

long long mod_pow(long long a, long long b) {
    long long result = 1;
    while (b > 0) {
        if (b & 1LL) result = result * a % MOD;
        a = a * a % MOD;
        b >>= 1LL;
    }
    return result;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n;
    if (!(cin >> n)) return 0;
    long long ans = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        long long p, q, v;
        cin >> p >> q >> v;
        ans = (ans + (v % MOD) * (p % MOD) % MOD * mod_pow(q, MOD - 2)) % MOD;
    }
    cout << ans << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


MOD = 1_000_000_007


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    n = data[0]
    idx = 1
    ans = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        p, q, v = data[idx], data[idx + 1], data[idx + 2]
        idx += 3
        ans = (ans + v % MOD * p % MOD * pow(q, MOD - 2, MOD)) % MOD
    print(ans)
```

# B. First Success

## Restatement

Repeated independent attempts succeed with probability `p/q`. Compute the
expected number of attempts until the first success.

## Algorithm and proof

Let `E` be the expected number of attempts. One attempt is always made. If it
fails, with probability `1-p/q`, the process restarts.

```text
E = 1 + (1-p/q)E
(p/q)E = 1
E = q/p
```

So print `q * inverse(p)`.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;

long long mod_pow(long long a, long long b) {
    long long result = 1;
    while (b > 0) {
        if (b & 1LL) result = result * a % MOD;
        a = a * a % MOD;
        b >>= 1LL;
    }
    return result;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int t;
    if (!(cin >> t)) return 0;
    while (t--) {
        long long p, q;
        cin >> p >> q;
        cout << q % MOD * mod_pow(p, MOD - 2) % MOD << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys

MOD = 1_000_000_007

data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
t = data[0]
idx = 1
out = []
for _ in range(t):
    p, q = data[idx], data[idx + 1]
    idx += 2
    out.append(str(q % MOD * pow(p, MOD - 2, MOD) % MOD))
print("\n".join(out))
```

# C. Coupon Collector

## Restatement

With `n` equally likely coupon types, compute the expected number of draws to
collect all types.

## Algorithm

When `i` types are already collected, the probability of getting a new type is
`(n-i)/n`, so the expected waiting time for the next new type is `n/(n-i)`.

Summing:

```text
answer = n * (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n)
```

Precompute modular harmonic sums.

## Correctness proof

The collection process splits into `n` stages: going from `i` collected types to
`i+1`. Each stage is a geometric wait with success probability `(n-i)/n`, so
its expected length is `n/(n-i)`. Expectations add, giving the formula.
`\square`

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;

long long mod_pow(long long a, long long b) {
    long long result = 1;
    while (b > 0) {
        if (b & 1LL) result = result * a % MOD;
        a = a * a % MOD;
        b >>= 1LL;
    }
    return result;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int q;
    if (!(cin >> q)) return 0;
    vector<int> values(q);
    int limit = 0;
    for (int &n : values) {
        cin >> n;
        limit = max(limit, n);
    }
    vector<long long> harmonic(limit + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 1; i <= limit; i++) {
        harmonic[i] = (harmonic[i - 1] + mod_pow(i, MOD - 2)) % MOD;
    }
    for (int n : values) cout << n * harmonic[n] % MOD << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys

MOD = 1_000_000_007
data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
q = data[0]
values = data[1 : 1 + q]
limit = max(values)
harmonic = [0] * (limit + 1)
for i in range(1, limit + 1):
    harmonic[i] = (harmonic[i - 1] + pow(i, MOD - 2, MOD)) % MOD
print("\n".join(str(n * harmonic[n] % MOD) for n in values))
```

# Testing discussion

Random tests use exact rational arithmetic with Python `Fraction`, then convert
the result to modular form. This catches the common mistake of using floating
point or rounding.

# What to carry forward

Expected value problems are often easier than distribution problems. Try
linearity first; if the process has repeated waiting for success, look for a
geometric stage.
